Markdown source: docs/README.md

Light Cycle – Documentation #

A Commodore 64 version of Light Cycle, the two-player light-cycle game for the Oric-1 and Atmos (16K or 48K) written by A.J. Clarke and published on tape by PSS in 1983. The game was written on an original Oric-1, by hand on paper, and entered with a machine code monitor (original_release.md). The C64 version runs the Oric game logic on a new C64 platform layer. The Oric original is kept alongside it: the tape, CYCLE.TAP, and its full commented source in oric/, which make verify assembles back into a byte-identical tape for any Oric emulator.

LIGHT_CYCLE.html gathers every document below, with the images embedded, into one page that reads offline in a browser.

Light Cycle – Player's Guide #

The rules are read from the Oric code (oric/game.s). The original has been run in Auric, but the rules have not been checked against it one by one. The C64 version follows the same rules, apart from the differences listed in porting.md.

Menus #

After loading, the title screen explains the keys. The game then asks, in order:

  1. Volume. A rainbow bar with a ~ marker: cursor up and down move it while a test tone plays; RETURN accepts. Volume 0 silences the game (VolumeScreen).
  2. Number of players. 1 puts the computer in charge of player 2; 2 gives player 2 to a second person (AskPlayers).
  3. Speed. 1 (fast) to 9 (slow): it sets the per-frame delay (AskSpeed, FrameDelay).

On the C64 the game opens with a picture after the original cassette inlay, then the instructions, then a demo of the computer playing itself; 1, SPACE or fire starts a one-player game and 2 a two-player one from any of them. Until the menus are ported (Phase 4) the volume is fixed at 10 and the speed at 5, and RUN/STOP ends a game. The scores, lives and TIME are in a panel on each side of the arena, laid out like the Oric's status rows: player 1 on the left, player 2 on the right. When a player runs out of lives the winner's name flashes, then the game returns to the intro (the hi-score table arrives in Phase 4).

Controls #

Control Oric P1 Oric P2 C64 P1 C64 P2
Up 2 ] 2 @
Down A Right SHIFT A Right SHIFT
Left W ; W :
Right E ' E ;
Boost R L R L

The C64 keys keep the Oric layout's shape; the C64 has no ] or '. Joystick port 2 also drives player 1, and port 1 player 2, with fire as boost (ReadKeysP1, ReadKeysP2 in c64/src/input.s).

Rules #

Each player rides a light cycle that leaves a permanent trail. Touching any lit pixel crashes. Player 1 starts at x=25 heading right, player 2 at x=215 heading left, both at random heights (RandomStarts).

The arena is a one-pixel frame (x 6–239, y 0–199) with a V-shaped wedge of random size at the middle of each wall, pointing inward (DrawObstacles), on a random paper colour: red, blue, magenta or black (SetPaperColour). Every 255 frames BonusBlocks tries a random empty 6×6 spot and animates a block there; the last frame stays as a new obstacle, so the arena slowly fills.

Normal speed moves a cycle one pixel every second frame; boost moves it every frame. Player 2's trail is dotted (plotted on alternate steps), so the two trails can be told apart in monochrome.

Scoring and Winning #

TIME counts up every 8 frames at speeds 1–3 and every 4 frames at speeds 4–9 (TickTime). When a player crashes, the other scores TIME + 200 and TIME restarts (AwardP1, AwardP2). Each player has 5 lives. When either has none left, the higher score wins (DecideWinner): the winner's name flashes and their score goes to the hi-score table of eight, LIGHT CYCLE HEROES. If the computer wins, it types its own name. SPACE plays again; V returns to the volume screen (PlayAgain).

The Computer #

ComputerAI looks 3 pixels ahead, 3 pixels wide. When the way is blocked it turns toward player 1 on the other axis; AIAvoid reverses that turn if it is blocked too. AIBoost boosts whenever the computer is 30 or more pixels from player 1 on either axis, so it closes distance fast and slows down near player 1.

Light Cycle – The Original Release #

How It Was Written #

A.J. Clarke wrote Light Cycle in 1983 on an original Oric-1. The program was written out by hand on paper and then entered into the Oric with a machine code monitor. PSS published it on cassette, and everything in this repository starts from that tape. The release is catalogued on Oric.org.

The Cassette Instructions #

The instruction sheet packed with the PSS cassette, printed on the Oric's own printer. It carries the same text as the game's title screen: the PSS logo and address, both players' keys drawn as a compass, the one-player rule and the author credit.

The keys on the sheet are the ones the disassembly reads, and the C64 port keeps their shape (player_guide.md):

Player Up Left Right Down Boost
Player 1 2 W E A R
Player 2 ] ; ' Right SHIFT L

The PSS Advert #

A full-page PSS advert, "Real Software for your Oric 1", with the Light Cycle inlay in the top-left corner. Light Cycle is listed under "Available soon" at £6.95, beside Centipede, Invaders, Hopper, Oric-Mon and The Ultra. Its blurb sells the Tron setting (the M.C.P. and the grid), one or two players against each other or the computer, and 100% machine code.

The Reviews #

Two reviews and a New Releases column, cut down to the Light Cycle pieces.

The long review lists the game for the 16K or 48K Oric, from PSS at £5.95. It walks through the volume, players and speed questions, the boost key, the on-screen timer and the nine-name Light Cycle Heroes table, and calls the randomly placed blocks "Rom towers". The caption sums it up: "good value for money".

The boxed review, signed M.C., lists the game as Light Cycle ORIC-1 at £6.95 and gives it five stars:

Rating Score
Instructions 75%
Playability 80%
Graphics 85%
Value for money 85%

It singles out the adjustable volume, given how loud the Oric's sound is.

A "New Releases" column introduces the game under the heading Light Bike, at £6.95, with the PSS inlay photographed and its "Arcade action for ORIC 1" strip. The column says PSS first issued the program on the Spectrum.

The Screens in the Review #

The long review's two photographs show the tape version this repository disassembles, not a different one: the arena, the wedge at the middle of each wall, and the three text rows under the HIRES screen that DrawStatusLine ($0BC4) fills from StatusText ($0454).

The same screen captured from the running game, one player against the computer partway into a round:

graphics.md (The Status Layout) compares it with the C64 panels.

Photograph Disassembly
PLAYER 1 and cycle icon, left StatusText ($0454)
TIME in a white box, centre Attributes $00, $17: black on white
COMPUTER and cycle icon, right StatusP2Name ($0472), or PLAYER 2
Big digits in a green box under TIME TimeAttrL ($0488): double height, green
000 and 5 each side Scores and lives, rows 1–2

The arena is 200 pixels high on both machines, and the C64 screen has no rows under it, so the port stacks each player's half of the status rows in a panel on their side: the same white TIME box over double-height digits on green, the names in the same colours beside the cycle icon, lives under the icon and the score under the name. Only the names are shortened, to P1, P2 and CPU, to fit five cells. graphics.md compares the two layouts in full and says why the C64 one differs.

Markdown source: docs/graphics.md

Light Cycle – Screens and Graphics #

The Oric figures are decoded from the tape by docs/tools/render_graphics.py; the C64 screenshots are VICE captures of the current build by docs/tools/capture_screens.py (see html_documentation.md). Oric figures are drawn 6 pixels per character cell, as the Oric displays them, and enlarged ×4.

The Oric Display #

The game plays in HIRES: 240×200 pixels at $A000, 40 bytes per line, each byte holding 6 pixels (bits 5–0) with bit 6 set. A byte with bit 6 clear is a serial attribute instead: it sets the ink or paper colour for the rest of the line. Column 0 of every line holds the paper attribute chosen by SetPaperColour, which is why the arena frame starts at x=6. Below the bitmap, three text rows at $BF68 show names, lives, TIME and scores. Menus and the hi-score table use TEXT mode (40×28 characters at $BB80), with serial attributes for colour, double height and the alternate character set.

CharsetToHires and CharsetToText copy the character set between $B400 (TEXT) and $9800 (HIRES) whenever the mode changes, because the HIRES bitmap covers the TEXT character set's address (architecture.md).

Decoded Figures #

The title screen's logo is the publisher's: PSS, drawn in the alternate character set from glyphs that LoaderStart copies to $B900 (AltGlyphs).

The status rows show a small cycle beside each player's lives: GlyphBike, defined into characters { and | by DefineGlyphs. The same routine defines } and ~ from GlyphArrows, used by the volume screen.

BonusBlocks animates each new obstacle through five frames of BonusGfx, in the order BonusFrameOfs gives; the last frame stays on screen.

Explosion sends 32 particles from the crash point (red) toward targets offset by ExplodeDX and ExplodeDY (yellow). Each waits a random 5–20 ticks, then travels one Bresenham step per tick as a single moving dot, unplotting the pixel it leaves, until it reaches its target or the arena's edge. Particles therefore nibble small gaps in the trails and walls they cross.

C64 Build #

The intro picture is new to the C64 version: a multicolour bitmap after the original PSS cassette inlay, drawn by tools/make_intro.py with the PSS logo decoded from the tape. Below is the generator's preview (pixels doubled in width, as multicolour mode shows them), then the picture as VICE shows it.

The attract cycle then shows the instructions (a placeholder until the Phase 4 menus) and runs demo mode: the computer against itself, both panels marked CPU. The arena, its wedges, the trails (player 2's dotted) and the bonus blocks are the Oric's, drawn by the ported code.

The side panels hold the Oric's status rows, rearranged: the next section says how and why.

The Status Layout: Oric and C64 #

The one visible change to the game's screen on the C64 is where the scores, lives and TIME go.

The Oric Original #

The Oric shows its arena on a 240×200 HIRES screen, and the last three lines of the display stay in text mode. The game writes its status into those three rows (DrawStatusLine, $0BC4, from StatusText, $0454), across the full width under the arena, as the long review photographed it in 1983 (original_release.md).

The photograph is too soft to read. Here is the same screen captured from the running game (one player against the computer, partway into a round; pixels ×2), with the Oric's own ROM font:

The figures below are a replica built from the game itself, to tie each part of that screen to the disassembly: render_graphics.py runs the Oric's ResetScores, ResetTime, RoundStart and the first frames of GameLoop on the 6502 core in tools/cpu6502.py, then draws the resulting HIRES memory and status rows with the Oric's serial attributes (ink, paper, double height). The arena, wedges, trails, colours, icon and layout are therefore the original's, byte for byte. One thing is not: the Oric ROM font is not on the tape, so letters and digits use the C64 font squeezed to the Oric's five-pixel width. The round is chosen to have black paper, as in the capture.

Row Left Centre Right
0 PLAYER 1 and cycle icon TIME, black on a white box Cycle icon and COMPUTER
1 – TIME digits, top half –
2 Score, and lives under icon TIME digits, bottom half Lives under icon, and score

Player 1's name is yellow and player 2's (COMPUTER or PLAYER 2) cyan; scores and lives are white. The TIME digits are double height, black on a green box. The rows take the round's random paper colour, like the arena. At the end of a match the winner's name is toggled in inverse 25 times.

The C64 Version #

The C64 has no spare rows: its bitmap is 320×200, and the arena's 200 lines fill it. What it has is width. The arena keeps the Oric's 240-pixel coordinates, centred, which leaves 40 pixels (five character cells) each side. So each player's half of the status rows is stacked in the panel on their side, at the foot of the panel as the rows were at the foot of the Oric screen (hud.s):

Panel row Shows As the Oric
16 TIME, black on a white box Row 0, centre
17–18 TIME digits, double height, black on green Rows 1–2, centre (BitmapCharTall)
20 Name and cycle icon Row 0, left or right
21 Lives, under the icon Row 2, under the icon
22 Score, last five of its eight digits Row 2, under the name

Left panel: name then icon, as the Oric's left half; right panel: icon then name, as its right half. The colours, the paper colour, the icon (the Oric's own glyphs from the tape) and the 25 inverse toggles of the winner's name are the Oric's.

What Differs, and Why #

Oric C64 Why
Three rows under the arena A panel each side, rows stacked No rows free under a 200-line arena
One TIME box, centre A TIME box in each panel The centre is the arena; keeps symmetry
PLAYER 1, PLAYER 2, COMPUTER P1, P2, CPU Eight characters; a panel has five
Six TIME digits, eight per score Five of each shown Five cells; all eight digits are kept
Text characters with attributes Glyphs drawn into the bitmap The C64 bitmap has no text rows

Two other layouts were considered and rejected. Shrinking the arena to make room under it would change the game: every coordinate, wall and wedge position, and the computer's play, depend on the 240×200 grid. Opening the lower border to show the rows with sprites would need a raster-timed border trick, eight sprites too few to carry 40 characters, and separate PAL and NTSC timing; it adds a lot of code for the same information. The panels use space the C64 otherwise leaves empty and keep the Oric's arena exactly.

Markdown source: docs/sound.md

Light Cycle – Sound #

The Oric game has no music: it has two engine drones, a start-of-round sweep, a volume test tone and an explosion. All of it is written straight to the AY-3-8912 through the VIA (AyWrite, AyLoadAll). The C64 version replaces each with a SID routine in c64/src/sound.s. No recordings yet: the C64 sounds have only been checked to build, not tuned by ear.

The Oric Driver #

AyWrite writes register A with value X: the register number goes out on VIA port A and is latched by setting the PCR's CA2/CB2 lines (AY BC1/BDIR), then the value follows the same way. Writes to R7, the mixer, always keep bit 6 set, because AY port A carries the keyboard column select. AyLoadAll writes R0–R13 from a 14-byte table.

Effect Oric routine What it writes
Engines EngineSound Tone A (P1), tone B (P2); period $05FE, $0480 boosted
Round start StartSweep Periods fall from $4FE (A) and $5FF (B) to ~`$101`
Volume test tone VolumeScreen Tone A, period $047F, at the chosen volume
Explosion Explosion ExplodeAY: noise on all channels, tones off, envelope

An AY tone of period P plays at 1 MHz ÷ 16P, so the engines drone at about 41 Hz, rising to 54 Hz while boosting. EngineSound only retunes a channel when that player's boost state changes. The explosion table sets noise period $1F (the lowest), envelope period $1904 and shape $01, a single decay of about 1.6 s. It is skipped when the volume is 0.

The SID Equivalents #

The SID value for frequency f is f × 2²⁴ ÷ 985248 on a PAL machine, so an AY period P becomes 1064250 / P (SIDFREQ in sound.s). NTSC machines play about 4% sharp; that is not corrected.

Oric C64 How
EngineSound EngineTone Voices 1 and 2, 50% pulse, the same two pitches
StartSweep StartSweep 64 steps × 2 frames (~2.6 s), the same period ramp
Explosion ExplosionSfx Voice 3 noise, decay 1.5 s to sustain 0; engines gated off
R8/R9 volume SetVolume SID master volume $D418, also 0–15

The engines use the SID's envelope only as a gate (attack 0, sustain 15), as the AY tones had fixed volume. Demo mode runs with the volume at 0, so it is silent and, as on the Oric with no volume, skips the start sweep.

Markdown source: docs/architecture.md

Light Cycle – Architecture #

How the Oric original is put together, read from the disassembly, and how the C64 port is laid out. Oric addresses are 48K addresses; the 16K behaviour is covered below.

Tape and Boot #

CYCLE.TAP holds two Oric tape blocks (data_formats.md). The first, LIGHT CYCLE, is a BASIC program loaded at $0501. Its six lines set TEXT:INK7:PAPER0, run CALL #900 and then CLOAD"". LoaderStart at $0900 uses BlockCopy three times: 64 logo glyphs to the alternate character set at $B900, two chevron glyphs to $B7E0, and the finished title and instructions screen to $BB80. While the player reads it, CLOAD"" loads the second block, GAME, at $0400–$1800. It overwrites the BASIC program and autoruns at Entry ($0400), which jumps to Start.

Hardware Use (Oric) #

The game makes no ROM calls. It drives the hardware itself and borrows a few ROM workspace bytes.

Area How the game uses it
Display HIRES 240×200 at $A000 plus three text rows
Mode switch Writes $1E (HIRES) or $1A (TEXT) to $BFDF
Keyboard Play: direct matrix scan via VIA port B and AY port A
Menu keys ROM IRQ handler; WaitKey reads ROM_KEY ($02DF)
Sound AY-3-8912 through VIA port A and the PCR
Timing Busy-wait loops (FrameDelay, Delay)
Randomness Additive generator over $D0–$D3 (Random)

RoundStart masks interrupts and ViaGameSetup turns the VIA timer interrupt off, so during play the keys are read straight from the matrix by ReadKeysP1 and ReadKeysP2. A crash calls ViaRestoreRom, which recreates the ROM's 100 Hz timer setup, so the menus and name entry can use the ROM keyboard again.

The "16K OR 48K" line in the BASIC stub works, probably, because a 16K Oric repeats its RAM through the address space: HIRES $A000 lands on $2000 and the HIRES character set $9800 on $1800, directly after the code. That is inferred from the addresses chosen, not tested.

Memory Map (Oric, 48K) #

Range Use
$0000–$0008 Scratch
$0030–$0068 Game state (the zero-page map at the top of game.s)
$0400–$06BF Tables and text; Entry at $0400
$06C0–$17C8 Code
$9800–$9EFF The TEXT character set, moved here while in HIRES
$9D00–$9E5F Explosion particle state, 11 tables × 32
$A000–$BF3F HIRES bitmap (column 0 = paper attribute)
$B800–$B8DF Hi-score table, 8 × 28 bytes
$B900/$B920 Winner's score and name for HiscoreEntry
$BB80–$BFDF TEXT screen: menus and hi-scores
$BF68–$BFDF HIRES-mode text rows: names, TIME, lives, scores

The character-set shuffle is the subtlest part. Entering HIRES, CharsetToHires copies $B400–$BAFF to $9800–$9EFF, because the HIRES bitmap overlays the TEXT character set. Leaving it, CharsetToText copies it back. The hi-score table at $B800 rides along in the alternate set's area. Before the copy back, DecideWinner stores the winner's score and name at $9D00 and $9D20, so they arrive at NEW_SCORE and NEW_NAME ($B900, $B920) ready for HiscoreEntry.

Program Flow #

MovePlayer runs once per player per frame. It reads the keys (or ComputerAI and AIBoost for a one-player game), skips odd frames unless boosting, accepts a new direction only when exactly one direction key is down, erases the three-pixel head (EraseHead), steps one pixel, then tests and redraws the head with PlotCheckCrash. A crash jumps straight out of the two subroutine levels to the next round (quirks.md).

The C64 Port #

The C64 version runs on a platform layer that takes the machine over completely (platform_layer.md): BASIC and the KERNAL are banked out, the CIA interrupts are off, and one raster interrupt per frame counts ticks. The video memory sits in VIC bank 1, so text screen, font and bitmap never overlap and the Oric's character-set shuffle is not needed.

Range Use
$0002–$00FF Zero page (all free: no KERNAL)
$0801–$080C BASIC stub 10 SYS 2061
$080D–$3FFF Code, tables, variables
$4400–$47E7 Text screen (menus)
$4800–$4FFF Font (a copy of the ROM font for now)
$5C00–$5FE7 Bitmap colours: ink and paper per 8×8 cell
$6000–$7F3F Hires bitmap, 320×200
$C000–$C0FF Hi-score table (reserved)
$FFFA–$FFFF NMI and IRQ vectors (RAM under the KERNAL)

The game keeps the Oric's 240×200 coordinates. The arena is drawn 40 pixels in from the left of the 320-pixel bitmap, leaving a 40-pixel panel each side for the status rows the Oric showed under its bitmap.

The status panels (hud.s) replace the Oric's three text rows: player 1's half of them (name, cycle icon, lives, score, and the TIME box) is stacked at the foot of the 5 cells left of the arena, player 2's on the right, in the Oric's colours and on the round's paper.

RunTick waits for the raster tick, then runs OricFrame (the body of the Oric's GameLoop) as many times as the Oric would have in that time (porting.md). PlotCheckCrash sets zCrashed and returns out of MovePlayer, so the crash is handled by the caller with the stack intact.

Markdown source: docs/data_formats.md

Light Cycle – Data Formats #

The tape format and the Oric game's tables, read from the code. Labels are the disassembly's (tools/symbols.py).

Tape Blocks #

Each Oric tape block is a run of $16 sync bytes, $24, a 9-byte header, a 0-terminated name, then the data. The end address is inclusive. tools/tap_extract.py splits CYCLE.TAP this way, and tools/build_tap.py writes the assembled source back out the same way (make verify).

Header byte Meaning LIGHT CYCLE GAME
0–1 Unused $00 $EC $34 $EC
2 Type: $00 BASIC, $80 machine code $00 $80
3 Autorun flag $04 $04
4–5 End address, high byte first $0E80 $1800
6–7 Start address, high byte first $0501 $0400
8 Unused $FF $FF

HIRES Pixel Bytes #

A HIRES byte with bit 6 set holds six pixels, bit 5 on the left. HiresAddr turns a pixel (x, y) into an address and a mask: $A000 + 40y + x div 6, and PixelMask[x mod 6] ($60 $50 $48 $44 $42 $41, bit 6 kept set). ClearHires fills with $40, an empty pixel byte.

Tables in the GAME Block #

Label Address Size Holds
ViaRegIdx $0424 7 VIA registers ViaGameSetup writes (overlaps next)
ViaRegVal $042A 7 Their values
BonusRowOfs $0430 6 Row offsets ×40 for the 6-line bonus block
BonusGfx $0436 24 Four 6-byte frames: three shapes and a blank
BonusFrameOfs $044E 6 Animation order as offsets into BonusGfx
StatusText $0454 40 HIRES status row 0, with attributes; P2 name at $0472
TimeAttrL/R $0488 3+3 Attributes around TIME: double height, black on green
ExplodeDX $0490 32 Particle target x offsets, signed
ExplodeAY $04B0 14 AY R0–R13 for the explosion
ExplodeDY $04C0 32 Particle target y offsets, signed
GlyphBike $04F0 16 Characters 123–124: the status-row cycle
GlyphArrows $0550 16 Characters 125–126: down arrow, slider marker
PixelMask $05A1 6 HIRES bit per x mod 6
HiDefault $0608 17 Default hi-score entry
PaperColours $0619 4 Paper attributes: red, blue, magenta, black
RankInk $0620 8 Ink attribute per hi-score rank
KeyRowP1… $06A0 3×5 P1 keys: matrix row, column mask, zInput bit
KeyRowP2… $06AF 3×5 P2 keys, same layout

Text tables (menus, prompts, the play-again rows) hold serial attributes inline: $00–$07 set ink, $08–$0F the character set and double height, $10–$17 paper. Each attribute takes a character cell and shows as a space.

Status Rows #

In HIRES mode the three text rows start at HIRES_STATUS0 ($BF68), HIRES_STATUS1 and HIRES_STATUS2. Scores and TIME are 8-character ASCII numbers kept in screen memory and added to digit by digit with AddDigit, which treats a leading space as 0.

Field Row Columns Address
P1 score 2 2–9 $BFBA–$BFC1
P1 lives 2 12 $BFC4
TIME 1–2 15–22 $BF9F, $BFC7
P2 lives 2 27 $BFD3
P2 score 2 30–37 $BFD6–$BFDD

TIME is written to both rows 1 and 2 under a double-height attribute. The C64 keeps these fields in RAM in the same form (ScoreP1, ScoreP2, TimeDigits: 8 ASCII characters, right-aligned, spaces before the first digit; LivesP1, LivesP2: one ASCII digit) and draws them into its side panels.

Hi-Score Entry #

HISCORE_TAB ($B800) holds 8 entries of 28 bytes; InitHiscores writes 9 from HiDefault. Bytes 0–7 are the score (compared on bytes 1–7), byte 8 onward the name, ended by $0D. The default entry is a score of 500 and the name P.S.S.. PrintHiscores shows rank, score, --- and the name, in the rank's ink from RankInk.

Light Cycle – Source Guide and Toolchain #

Repository #

Path Holds
CYCLE.TAP The original Oric tape: the reference for everything else
oric/game.s Annotated disassembly of the GAME block (generated, committed)
oric/loader.s Annotated disassembly of the LIGHT CYCLE block
oric/light_cycle.bas The BASIC stub as text
tools/ Tape, disassembly, tape rebuild, timing, table export, intro tools
build/ CYCLE.TAP assembled from oric/*.s (make tap): never committed
c64/src/ The C64 port (ca65)
c64/cfg/c64.cfg ld65 memory layout
c64/build/ Build output, screenshots: never committed
docs/ These chapters, the handbook and its tools

Toolchain #

Tool Used for
cc65 (ca65, ld65, da65) Assembling the port; disassembling the Oric code
VICE (x64sc, c1541) Running and capturing the port; the .d64
Python 3 Tape and disassembly tools (standard library)
Pillow (Homebrew python3.14) Decoding the Oric figures
Node.js 20+ Generating the HTML handbook
just Documentation recipes

Building #

The Makefile builds the C64 version and the Oric tape; the justfile wraps it and adds the documentation recipes (html_documentation.md).

Command Does
make c64/build/lightcycle.prg, plus lightcycle.map and the VICE label file
make d64 c64/build/lightcycle.d64
make run Starts the build in VICE with the labels loaded into its monitor
make smoke Headless boot; screenshots into c64/build/ (capture_screens.py)
make oric Splits the tape, regenerates oric/*.s, checks they rebuild byte for byte
make tap build/CYCLE.TAP from oric/loader.s and oric/game.s (tools/build_tap.py)
make verify make tap, then checks build/CYCLE.TAP byte for byte against CYCLE.TAP
make oric-run Loads build/CYCLE.TAP in Auric, Oric-1 mode (AURIC_DIR)
make intro Redraws c64/src/intro.rle and its preview (tools/make_intro.py)
make tables Re-exports c64/src/oric_tables.inc (tools/export_tables.py)
make clean Removes c64/build/ and build/

make oric must report both blocks as IDENTICAL. It runs tools/tap_extract.py, then tools/build_disasm.py, which writes a da65 info file from tools/symbols.py, disassembles, adds the comments and reassembles with cl65. Labels and comments are changed in tools/symbols.py followed by make oric; oric/*.s is never edited by hand. make verify then wraps the two assembled blocks in the original tape headers and confirms the tape matches.

C64 Source Conventions #

  • One module per concern, each starting with a comment naming the Oric routines it replaces or ports. Platform: platform.s, video.s, plot.s, timing.s, input.s, sound.s. Game: game.s (rounds, timing budget), player.s, ai.s, arena.s, explosion.s, bonus.s, score.s, hud.s. Front end: main.s (attract cycle, demo), intro.s. Where a routine takes over an Oric routine's job, it keeps its name and its register contract.
  • Ported game code follows the Oric line for line, including where it relies on the carry flag; changes are listed in porting.md and marked in the comments.
  • Generated sources are committed and never edited: oric_tables.inc (tools/export_tables.py) and intro.rle (tools/make_intro.py).
  • Hardware addresses, memory layout and constants live in hw.inc; zero page is declared in zp.s and imported through zp.inc. No raw hardware addresses in code.
  • Lookup tables are generated at assembly time with .repeat, so the arithmetic that defines them is in the source.
  • basic_stub.s links first so Start lands at $080D; an .assert fails the link otherwise.
  • Strings for the text screen use screencodes.inc and end with STR_END ($FF), because @ is screen code 0.
  • The BSS segment is zeroed by ClearBss at start-up: the loader leaves RAM as it was.

Reference

Markdown source: docs/porting.md

Light Cycle – Porting to the C64 #

The plan for the Commodore 64 version and where it stands. Both machines run a ~1 MHz 6502, so the game logic (movement, the computer player, lines, the explosion, bonus blocks, scoring, the random generator) ports almost instruction for instruction. The work is the platform underneath: display, keyboard, sound, timing and the menu screens.

Approach #

The port is a faithful re-host, not a rewrite. It keeps the structure and names of oric/game.s, so each C64 routine can be checked against its Oric original, and replaces only the platform routines behind a small interface (platform_layer.md). Improvements (sprites, disk hi-scores) come after a faithful version plays correctly. The toolchain is cc65: the disassembly is already ca65 syntax, and VICE runs and captures the builds.

Status #

Phase Scope State
0 Repository, build, boot stub Done 16-11-2026
1 Platform layer and test harness Done 16-11-2026, see below
2 Game logic, demo mode, intro picture Done 16-11-2026, see below
3 Status panels, scoring, lives, winner Done 16-11-2026, see below
4 Menus, title, hi-scores Next
5 Polish: sprites, joystick options, NTSC, disk hi-scores Optional
6 Release: .prg, .d64, tag –

Phases 1–3 are verified by VICE captures (graphics.md) and by stopping VICE inside a crash: the intro picture, the instructions, demo mode drawing the Oric's arena, both computer players, the dotted trail, bonus blocks, crashes, the explosion and new rounds. Not yet tried by hand: the keyboard and joysticks in a real game, and the SID sounds. VICE's headless mode cannot press matrix keys, and its captures have no sound.

Phase 2: The Game Logic #

arena.s, player.s, ai.s, explosion.s and bonus.s are the Oric routines ported line for line under their Oric names (Random, DrawLine, DrawObstacles, RandomStarts, MovePlayer, EraseHead, PlotCheckCrash, ComputerAI, AIBoost, Explosion, BonusBlocks and the rest). Carry is kept where the Oric relies on it, so the same seed draws the same arena. The Oric's data tables are exported from the tape by tools/export_tables.py into c64/src/oric_tables.inc, not typed in by hand. The differences are:

Oric C64
PlotCheckCrash jumps out to the crash code Sets zCrashed, returns from MovePlayer (quirk 1)
The computer always chases P1 (zP1X, zP1Y) It chases zOppX, zOppY: the other cycle
Only P2 can be the computer zAI bit 0 = P1, bit 1 = P2: demo mode is both
BonusBlocks tests and writes whole HIRES bytes Tests and draws the same 6×6 area pixel by pixel
DrawBonusFrame borrows zSlowP1 as a counter Uses its own scratch byte (quirk 7)
Explosion state in spare charset RAM at $9D00 BSS tables
GameLoop padded by FrameDelay RunTick runs Oric frames against a time budget

Timing. tools/oric_timing.py runs the Oric's own RoundStart and GameLoop on a cycle-counting 6502 core (tools/cpu6502.py) until the first crash, for each speed, one or two players, with and without boost, over six seeds. The Oric runs at 1 MHz and its ULA takes no CPU time, so cycles are microseconds.

Speed Two players (µs/frame) One player (µs/frame) One player, P1 boosting Explosion
1 7213 11171 14819 1.48 s
5 12370 16328 19976 1.48 s
9 17506 21464 25112 1.48 s

So a frame costs 7213 µs + 1287 µs per speed step, plus ~3958 µs per computer player and ~3550 µs per boosting cycle. RunTick adds each C64 frame's length (19950 µs PAL, 16716 µs NTSC) to a budget and runs Oric frames while it lasts, charging each frame that cost. Every frame counter then runs at the Oric's rate: movement, bonus blocks, the computer's decisions. Two Oric effects carry over by design: a one-player game is slower than a two-player one, and boost is about 1.5 times normal speed rather than twice, because a boosting frame takes longer. At speed 5 a cycle travels about 31 pixels per second against the computer.

Demo mode. Left alone, the attract cycle runs the computer against itself (zAI = 3), silently, with scores and lives, for four crashes, until a player runs out of lives, or until a key or fire. With the volume at 0 the Oric skipped the round-start sweep, and so does the demo.

Intro picture. tools/make_intro.py draws a multicolour bitmap after the original PSS cassette inlay: the PSS logo (decoded from the tape), chrome LIGHT CYCLE lettering with a glint, a perspective grid, the light cycle with its yellow-green trail and flare, and a strapline that reads ARCADE ACTION FOR COMMODORE 64 where the inlay said ORIC 1. It is packed to about 5 KB (intro.rle) and unpacked into VIC bank 1 by IntroScreen.

Phase 3: Scores, Lives and the Winner #

score.s ports AddDigit, TickTime, the awards, ResetTime, ResetScores and DecideWinner. The Oric kept its numbers as ASCII digits in the status rows on screen and added to them there; the C64 keeps the same 8-character fields in RAM (ScoreP1, ScoreP2, TimeDigits) and lives as ASCII digits (LivesP1, LivesP2), and hud.s redraws a field when it changes. A crash runs the explosion, then AwardOpponent (the Oric's AwardP1 / AwardP2 and the lives update), then the pause; on a last life PlayGame calls DecideWinner and FlashWinner. Verified in VICE by setting both players to one life and letting the computers play: the right winner flashed, with its score.

Oric C64
Three text rows under the HIRES screen Each side's half stacked in a 5-cell panel, at its foot
TIME: white box, double height on green The same boxes in both panels (BitmapCharTall)
PLAYER 1 yellow, COMPUTER cyan P1 yellow, P2 or CPU cyan
Status rows on the arena's paper colour Panels on the arena's paper colour (ArenaPaper)
8-digit scores The last five digits shown; all eight kept
Cycle icon in characters 123–124 The same glyphs in two spare font characters
Winner's name toggled in inverse 25 times The same: 25 toggles, ending reversed
DecideWinner relies on a stray carry SEC first (quirk 2)

The layout change, with figures of both and the reasons, is in graphics.md (The Status Layout).

Platform Mapping #

Oric feature C64 replacement
HIRES 240×200, 6 px/byte Hires bitmap 320×200, 8 px/byte
HiresAddr (÷6 loop) Row and column lookup tables
Paper attribute in col 0 Bitmap colour cells, ink and paper per 8×8
3 text rows under HIRES Side panels drawn into the bitmap
TEXT mode, serial attrs Text mode and colour RAM
6×8 font, alt charset logo 8×8 font, logo re-gridded
VIA + AY matrix scan CIA1 matrix scan, plus joysticks
ROM IRQ keyboard (menus) GetKey / WaitKey, own matrix scan
AY tones A and B SID voices 1 and 2
AY noise and envelope SID voice 3 noise
Volume 0–15 SID master volume, also 0–15
Busy-wait FrameDelay Raster tick and a speed table
Character-set shuffle Not needed: VIC bank 1 keeps them apart
Particles, hi-scores in charset RAM Ordinary RAM

Decisions #

Arena geometry. The arena keeps the Oric's 240×200 coordinates, so every x fits in a byte and every constant carries over: start positions, the computer's look-ahead, the obstacle maths and the explosion bounds. It is drawn 40 pixels in on the 320-pixel bitmap, leaving a 40-pixel panel each side for what the Oric showed in its three text rows; a 200-line bitmap leaves no rows below it without a raster split.

Colour. A hires bitmap gives two colours per 8×8 cell, so two trails in one cell would clash. The port keeps player 2's dotted trail, as the Oric did, and colours a cell when a trail first enters it. Multicolour would avoid clashes but halve the horizontal resolution, making sideways movement twice as fast as vertical.

Timing. The Oric's speed came from a busy-wait plus a varying amount of drawing, so it was never constant. The C64 counts raster frames (50 Hz PAL, 60 Hz NTSC). Rather than a speed table tuned by eye, tools/oric_timing.py measures the Oric's own frame costs on a cycle-counting 6502 core, and RunTick runs Oric frames against that time budget (Phase 2, above). Every pixel step still runs the full crash test.

Controls. The Oric key layout, mapped by position (player_guide.md), plus joystick port 2 for player 1 and port 1 for player 2. Joystick 1 shares lines with the keyboard rows; ScanPlayerKeys masks the rows it holds down so it is not read as keys.

Title content. The Oric title screen carries the publisher's address under the PSS logo. Whether the C64 title keeps it, replaces it with a credit line or drops it is the owner's call; open.

Phases 4–6 #

Phases 2 and 3 are done and described under Status above. What remains:

Phase 4, menus. A converter in tools/ is to turn the Oric screens and strings (serial attributes, 6-pixel glyphs) into screen codes, colour RAM and 8×8 glyphs; the 28-row title has to fit 25 rows. Then VolumeScreen, AskPlayers, AskSpeed, HiscoreEntry, PrintHiscores, PlayAgain, FlashTitle. Exit test: title to game to hi-score and back.

Phase 5, polish (optional). Hardware sprites for the cycle heads, SID pulse-width movement on the engines, NTSC speed table, hi-scores saved to disk, exomizer packing.

Phase 6, release. .prg and .d64 attached to a GitHub release, the README's controls brought up to date, tag v1.0.

Risks #

Risk Mitigation
Speed and feel differ from Oric Measure the Oric; tune the speed table
Colour clash where trails cross Dotted P2 trail; first colour wins
6-pixel glyphs look wrong at 8 Redraw the logo and glyphs by hand
Title text needs 28 rows Reflow the instructions
AY timbre differs on the SID Tune by ear; semantic sound routines
Markdown source: docs/platform_layer.md

Light Cycle – Platform Layer #

The C64 routines the game logic calls instead of touching hardware (c64/src/). Where a routine does an Oric routine's job it keeps that name and register contract, so ported code calls it unchanged. Everything here is read from the source; the plotting, video and timing routines are also exercised by the game in VICE.

Start-Up and Timing #

InitPlatform (platform.s) takes the machine over once at start: interrupts off, BASIC and the KERNAL banked out ($01 = $35), CIA interrupts disabled, then InitVideo, InitTiming, InitInput and InitSound, and interrupts on. Nothing calls the ROMs afterwards. ClearBss (main.s) zeroes the variables.

Routine Module Contract
InitTiming timing.s Sets zIsPAL, IRQ/NMI vectors, raster IRQ on line 251
WaitTick timing.s Waits for the next frame; keeps X, Y
WaitTicks timing.s Waits X frames (0 = 256); keeps Y

The interrupt handler only acknowledges the VIC and increments zTick. RESTORE's NMI is ignored. PAL is told from NTSC by the highest raster line (312 lines against 263).

Video #

Routine Replaces (Oric) Contract
InitVideo – VIC bank 1, ROM font copied to $4800, black border
BitmapOn $1E to $BFDF Hires bitmap mode
TextOn $1A to $BFDF Text mode, black background
ClearBitmap ClearHires Zeroes $6000–$7FFF
ClearText ClearTextScreen A = screen code, X = colour
SetArenaColour SetPaperColour A = ink×16 + paper for arena cells
SetPanelColour – A = ink×16 + paper for both panels
SetCellColour – A = colour, X = column, Y = row; keeps X, Y
BitmapChar HIRES-mode text rows A = screen code into cell X, Y; keeps X, Y
BitmapCharTall Double-height attribute As BitmapChar, double height into Y and Y + 1
PrintText Menu text copies zPtr = string, X, Y = position, A = colour

CharsetToHires and CharsetToText have no equivalent: on the C64 the text screen ($4400), font ($4800), bitmap colours ($5C00) and bitmap ($6000) never overlap.

Plotting #

Coordinates are the Oric's (x 0–239, y 0–199); the arena is drawn ARENA_X_OFFSET (40) pixels in. Every lookup is a table generated at assembly time, against the Oric's divide-by-6 loop.

Routine Contract
HiresAddr X = x, Y = y → zPix, zMask; keeps A, X, Y
PlotPixel Sets the pixel at zPix/zMask; keeps X, Y
PlotXY Sets pixel X, Y; keeps X, Y
UnplotPixel Clears pixel X, Y; keeps X, Y
PixelSet C = 1 if pixel X, Y is lit; keeps X, Y

PixelSet is the Oric's PixelSet, and with PlotXY it covers PlotCheckCrash's test-then-plot.

Input #

Routine Replaces (Oric) Contract
ReadKeysP1 ReadKeysP1 Keys 2 A W E R + joystick 2 → zInput and A; X clobbered
ReadKeysP2 ReadKeysP2 Keys @ RSHIFT : ; L + joystick 1 → zInput and A
GetKey – New key code or 0; codes as the Oric's (KEY_* in hw.inc)
WaitKey WaitKey Blocks for a new key; code in A
ReadFire – C = 1 while fire is held on either joystick

zInput keeps the Oric bits: IN_UP $08, IN_DOWN $04, IN_LEFT $02, IN_RIGHT $01, IN_BOOST $10. The key tables (KeyTableP1, KeyTableP2) have the Oric layout: column, row mask and input bit per key. GetKey scans all 64 keys, returns a code only on a new press, and maps SHIFT with the cursor keys to KEY_UP and KEY_LEFT, as the Oric's separate cursor keys gave. Pressing keys while moving joystick 2 can show ghost keys; joystick 1 is masked.

Sound #

sound.md shows how each Oric effect maps to the SID.

Routine Replaces (Oric) Contract
InitSound – Silences the SID; voices set up; volume 0
SetVolume R8/R9 writes A = 0–15 → zVolume and the SID master volume
EnginesOn SoundInit Both engines gated on at normal pitch
EnginesOff – Both engines gated off
EngineTone EngineSound X = player, A = 0 boosting / 1 normal; keeps Y
StartSweep StartSweep Blocking ~2.6 s rise; leaves engines on
ExplosionSfx Explosion's AY table Engines off, noise burst with long decay

Zero Page #

Declared in zp.s, imported through zp.inc; with the KERNAL banked out all of $02–$FF is free.

Name Use
zTmp0–zTmp3 Scratch; any routine may change them
zPtr Two-byte scratch pointer
zPix, zMask HiresAddr result
zTick Frame counter
zIsPAL 1 = PAL, 0 = NTSC
zInput Player input bits
zLastKey GetKey's edge detection
zJoyIdle Port B with no column selected (joystick 1)
zVolume 0–15
Markdown source: docs/quirks.md

Light Cycle – Original Quirks #

Places where the Oric code does something unintended or fragile, read from the disassembly, with what the C64 port does about each. None is visible to a player as far as the code shows.

The List #

# Quirk Where C64 decision
1 A crash JMPs out of two JSR levels; 4 stack bytes leak PlotCheckCrash Fix: return a crash flag
2 Score comparison subtracts without SEC DecideWinner Fix: add SEC
3 Frame time varies with drawing load and speed setting FrameDelay Fix: raster ticks
4 Two routines are never called DeadClearStatus, DeadCharsetCopy Not ported
5 InitHiscores writes nine entries; eight are used InitHiscores Eight
6 Unreferenced tables and loader residue $0403, $047C, $04E0, $0975 Not ported
7 DrawBonusFrame uses zSlowP1 as its loop counter DrawBonusFrame Fix: own scratch byte
8 A bonus block mid-animation carries over to the next round RoundStart Kept
9 The explosion's moving dots erase the pixels they cross Explosion Kept
10 A carry out of a score's eighth digit writes before it AddDigit Kept (unreachable)
11 A tie goes to player 1 DecideWinner Kept

Notes #

1. SP is set only at cold start. Each crash leaves MovePlayer's and PlotCheckCrash's return addresses on the stack, and GameOver never resets it either. The 6502 stack wraps within page 1, so nothing breaks. On the C64, PlotCheckCrash sets zCrashed and returns from MovePlayer, and the game loop tests the flag.

2. The loop at DecideWinner relies on the carry left by the CMP #$30 that found a player out of lives, which is always set (equal). It works by accident.

3. FrameDelay waits zSpeed × 256 loop passes on top of the frame's work. Pixel plotting divides by 6 in a loop, so frames with more drawing run slower. The C64 version measures the Oric's frame times and runs Oric frames against a time budget on each raster tick, so the speed matches the Oric's on average without its jitter (porting.md).

5. The ninth entry ($B8E0) is never shown or compared.

7. Leaving zSlowP1 at $FF makes the next EngineSound see a change and retune player 1's engine for a frame until MovePlayer sets it again. Harmless, but there is no reason to copy it.

8. RoundStart does not reset zBonusState, so a block that was animating when a cycle crashed finishes its animation at the same spot in the new arena, even over a new wall or a start position.

9. Each explosion particle unplots its previous pixel, so it leaves small gaps in trails, walls and the arena frame. A cycle can later pass through such a gap.

10. AddDigit ripples a carry left with DEY / BPL; past digit 0 it stores at offset $FF. A score would need to pass 99,999,999 first.

11. DecideWinner declares player 1 the winner unless player 2's score is strictly higher.

Changelog #

[Unreleased] 17-11-2026 – Original release material, Oric-style panels #

Added #

  • A root README.md for the GitHub repository, in the same form as Hopper's. It presents the project as a C64 version of the game, with the Oric original and its source kept alongside and buildable for Oric emulators: the game, the C64 keys, C64 and Oric screenshots, the versions and the port's progress, the history, and how to build and run both.
  • make tap, make verify and make oric-run (with just verify and just oric-run): tools/build_tap.py assembles oric/loader.s and oric/game.s and wraps them in the original tape headers as build/CYCLE.TAP, which make verify checks byte for byte against CYCLE.TAP (it matches) and make oric-run loads in Auric. build/ is gitignored.
  • docs/original_release.md: how the game was written (1983, by hand on paper, entered with a machine code monitor), the PSS cassette instruction sheet, the PSS advert, two magazine reviews and a New Releases column cut to their Light Cycle parts, and the review's screen photographs matched against DrawStatusLine.
  • The 1983 origin in the README's opening paragraph and in credits.md.
  • BitmapCharTall (video.s): a glyph at double height over two cells, for the Oric's double-height TIME.
  • oric-game-screen.png: a capture of the Oric game screen with its own ROM font, in graphics.md (The Oric Original) and original_release.md (The Screens in the Review).
  • A link to the game's entry on Oric.org, in credits.md (Playing the Original) and original_release.md.
  • docs/oric.md, an appendix on the Oric for readers new to it: history, specifications, memory map, serial attributes and the three video modes, the AY-3-8912 and how the VIA reaches it, BASIC examples (run on the Atmos ROM in Auric), running the original in an emulator (Auric, ROMs from oric.free.fr), how Light Cycle uses the machine, and further reading. Its figures (oric-palette.png, oric-attributes.png, oric-envelopes.png) come from the new docs/tools/render_oric.py, run by just docs and just docs-graphics.

Changed #

  • Links to the Hopper repository (github.com/anthonyjclarke/Hopper-Oric) where the game is named: the README's history and original_release.md's advert.
  • A documentation pass across every chapter: everything is written in the third person; the docs index and README lead with the C64 version and point to the Oric original and its build; source_guide.md, data_formats.md and credits.md cover the tape rebuild; the player's guide no longer says the original is untested in an emulator; porting.md drops the superseded speed-table plan and the finished Phase 2 and 3 plans, keeping Phases 4–6.
  • The Oric appendix moves out of Reference into its own Appendix group in the handbook and index, and splits in two. oric_history.md ("History of Oric") is expanded into the full story: Tangerine and the Microtan, the Oric-1 and its French success, the 1983 factory fire, Edenspring and the Atmos, the peripherals, the Stratos and the receivers, Eureka and the Telestrat, the Pravetz 8D and Nova 64 clones, software and magazines, a timeline and today's community and hardware. oric_specs.md ("Oric Tech Specs") takes the specifications, memory map, graphics, sound and emulator sections, with new tables of the models and their storage. Both are general information on the Oric, with no game named, and the same files in every Oric reconstruction; the game's own screen gives way to an Auric capture of the HIRES BASIC example (oric-basic-hires.png). The founders are corrected to Paul Johnson, Mark Rainer and Nigel Penton Tilbury, with Barry Muncaster joining later.
  • The status panels follow the Oric's status rows, as the review photographs show them: TIME in black on a white box over double-height digits on green, P1 yellow and P2 / CPU cyan beside the cycle icon, lives under the icon, score under the name, all at the foot of the panel on the round's paper colour (ArenaPaper). The SCORE, LIVES and WINS labels are gone, and the winner's name toggles 25 times and stays reversed, as on the Oric.
  • The cycle icon's two halves now meet, as on the Oric.
  • graphics.md: "The Status Layout: Oric and C64", the Oric's status rows against the C64 panels, with figures cropped by render_graphics.py (status-oric.png, status-c64.png), what differs and why.
  • A replica of the Oric in-game screen (oric-screen.png) and its status rows, in place of the blurred review photograph: render_graphics.py runs the Oric's own RoundStart and first GameLoop frames on tools/cpu6502.py and draws the result with the Oric's serial attributes; letters use the C64 font squeezed to five pixels, since the Oric ROM font is not on the tape.

Fixed #

  • The handbook logo (bike-icon.png) drew the cycle icon's two characters with a 2-pixel gap, splitting it in two. The game prints { and | side by side (StatusText), so render_graphics.py now joins them (glyph_strip's gap=0).

Markdown source: docs/html_documentation.md

Light Cycle – Maintaining the Documentation #

Source of Truth #

The HTML handbook gathers the chapters in docs/, the changelog, the decoded figures and the VICE screenshots into one offline page. Images, styling, the reader's controls and the Mermaid renderer are all embedded, so it opens in a browser with no network access.

Edit the Markdown, never the generated HTML. Each chapter links to its Markdown source, and links between included documents become links within the page. Links to other repository files stay relative, so they work only when the checkout sits next to the HTML. The handbook has a contents sidebar, chapter search, image enlargement and print support.

The C64 Font Option #

The sidebar's Switch to the C64 font button sets the page in Style's C64 TrueType fonts. Their licence allows embedding them unmodified with @font-face but not offering the files for download, so docs/tools/fonts/ ignores everything but its own .gitignore. The option is included once C64_Pro-STYLE.woff2 and C64_Pro_Mono-STYLE.woff2 are copied from the package's fonts/ folder, unmodified, into docs/tools/fonts/. Without them the button is left out and just docs-check reports the handbook stale, because the committed handbook is generated with them. The paths and labels are retroFont in docs/handbook.json.

Regeneration #

The steps run from the repository root, in this order. The figure tool needs Pillow, which on the development Mac is Homebrew's /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.14.

Step Command Needs Writes
Split the tape, disassemble make oric cc65 oric/*.bin, oric/*.s
Build the C64 port make cc65 c64/build/lightcycle.prg
Capture the screens python3 docs/tools/capture_screens.py VICE (x64sc) docs/images/screens/
Decode the Oric figures python3 docs/tools/render_graphics.py Pillow, VICE docs/images/graphics/
Draw the appendix figures python3 docs/tools/render_oric.py Pillow docs/images/graphics/oric-*
Generate the HTML node docs/tools/build_docs.mjs Node.js 20+ docs/LIGHT_CYCLE.html
Check the HTML is current node docs/tools/build_docs.mjs --check Node.js 20+ –

The just recipes wrap them:

just docs

just docs runs every step. just docs-html only regenerates the HTML from the current Markdown and images, just docs-check fails if a chapter names a label that is not in the source or the saved HTML is stale, and just docs-watch regenerates it whenever a source changes. just docs-graphics and just docs-screens run one step. The recipes use DOCS_PYTHON, else Homebrew's python3.14, else python3.

How the Pictures Are Made #

  • Screenshots. capture_screens.py boots the build in a fresh headless x64sc (default settings, warp, no sound) for each capture and saves the screen after a fixed number of CPU cycles, with VICE's random autostart delay turned off. The attract cycle takes no input and demo mode starts from a fixed random seed, so the captures repeat exactly.
  • Oric figures. render_graphics.py reads the tape blocks extracted by make oric and finds every table by its label in tools/symbols.py. It draws glyphs 6 pixels wide, as the Oric does, and decodes the title logo's serial attributes for its colours. The Oric screen replica runs the game's own round set-up and first frames on tools/cpu6502.py and renders the memory with the Oric's attributes, borrowing VICE's C64 font for letters (the Oric ROM font is not on the tape); the status comparison crops the C64 side from the demo capture, so it runs after the screen captures. The figures are deterministic.
  • Oric appendix figures. render_oric.py draws the palette, a HIRES line of serial attributes and the AY's envelope shapes for oric_specs.md. It reads nothing from the game, so the file is the same in every Oric reconstruction.
  • Oric appendix screenshot. oric-basic-hires.png is a capture of oric_specs.md's HIRES BASIC example running in the Auric emulator on the Atmos ROM; it is not generated, so it is re-captured by hand if the example changes.

Chapter Selection and Presentation #

docs/handbook.json sets the title, the reading order and the groups. A new Markdown file appears only once it is listed there. docs/tools/build_docs.mjs does the conversion: it namespaces the headings by document, rewrites the links, embeds local images as data URIs, and fails on a broken link, a missing section or a remote image. Raw HTML in the Markdown is escaped. The layout and controls are docs/tools/handbook/handbook.html, handbook.css and handbook.js. Mermaid code blocks render in the browser, with the diagram's source under each one.

Generation is deterministic and has no timestamp. The "source revision" is the first 12 hex digits of a SHA-256 over the hashes of every input file, listed in the page's source-provenance block.

docs/tools/doc_names.py (just docs-names) fails if a chapter's code span names a label that is in neither the Oric disassembly nor the C64 source. Placeholders that only look like labels go in docs/tools/doc_names_ignore.txt.

Third-Party Renderers #

The generator uses Marked 17.0.5 to convert the Markdown, and the page embeds Mermaid 10.9.3 for the diagrams. Both are pinned and vendored in docs/tools/vendor/ with their licences, which are also reproduced in the handbook. The generator and the page templates are carried over unchanged from the Frak! and Thing On A Spring documentation.

Markdown source: docs/credits.md

Light Cycle – Credits and Links #

The Game #

Light Cycle for the Oric-1 and Atmos was written by A.J. Clarke. The game's own credit, on the title screen, reads AUTHOR - A.J.CLARKE, under the PSS logo and the publisher's address in Coventry; the default hi-score name is P.S.S.. It was written in 1983 on an original Oric-1, by hand on paper, and typed in with a machine code monitor (original_release.md). The C64 intro picture is drawn after the PSS cassette inlay for the Oric release; the inlay's artist is not yet credited here.

The Reconstruction #

The disassembly, its annotations and the C64 port are Anthony Clarke's project; the details of who did what are for the owner to fill in.

The Documentation #

These chapters and the handbook follow the documentation format of Anthony's C64 reconstructions (Frak!, Thing On A Spring). The handbook generator and templates are carried over from those repositories unchanged.

Tools #

Tool Use
cc65 ca65, ld65, da65, cl65
VICE x64sc emulation and captures, c1541
Auric Running the Oric original and the rebuild
Python Tape, disassembly and figure tools
Pillow Figure rendering
Node.js Handbook generation

Libraries and Fonts #

Marked 17.0.5 converts the Markdown and Mermaid 10.9.3 draws the diagrams; both are vendored with their licences in docs/tools/vendor/. The handbook's C64 font option uses Style's C64 TrueType fonts, embedded unmodified as their licence allows.

Playing the Original #

CYCLE.TAP runs in any Oric emulator that loads .tap files, such as Auric or Oricutron; where it does not start by itself, CLOAD"" loads it. make verify builds the same tape from the source in oric/, as build/CYCLE.TAP, and make oric-run starts it in Auric (oric_specs.md covers the ROMs and set-up).

The game's entry on Oric.org, the Oric software archive, lists the PSS release (1983, by A. J. Clarke) with in-game screenshots and the cassette cover.

Appendix

Markdown source: docs/oric_history.md

History of Oric #

An introduction to the Oric home computers for readers who know the C64 but not the Oric: where the machines came from, how they sold, what became of the company and who keeps them running today. The hardware itself is described in the next appendix, Oric Tech Specs.

The history comes from the English and French Wikipedia articles and the other sources under Further Reading. Where they disagree, as they often do on dates and sales, both figures are given. Both Wikipedia articles are flagged as short of citations, so treat exact numbers as approximate.

Tangerine and the Microtan (1979–1982) #

The Oric began at Tangerine Computer Systems, founded in 1979 in St Ives, Cambridgeshire, by Dr Paul Johnson, Mark Rainer and Nigel Penton Tilbury. Its first product was the TAN1648, a VDU kit, and its first computer the Microtan 65: one of the first 6502 kit computers, built as rack-mounted boards with a little RAM, a character generator and a UHF modulator, and expandable with a serial port, more memory and BASIC in ROM. A later design, the Microtan 2, was sold to the amplifier maker HH Electronics, which released it as the HH Tiger without much success. Tangerine also made Prestel adapters under the Tantel name.

Rainer and Penton Tilbury stepped back to consultancy work, Barry Muncaster joined the running of the company, and it moved to Ely. After the success of Sinclair's ZX Spectrum, Tangerine's backers suggested a cheap colour home computer. Tangerine set up Oric Products International in April 1982 to build one around the same 6502, and Tansoft (from "Tangerine Software") became its software label.

The Oric-1 (1982–1983) #

The Oric-1 went on sale in the UK in the autumn of 1982 (the English Wikipedia gives 1 September; other sources say 1983). It cost £129 with 16K of RAM and £169 with 48K, a few pounds under the 48K Spectrum, and offered what the Spectrum lacked: a proper sound chip, a printer port, and colour that did not clash in the Spectrum's way, though it had limits of its own.

It sold well. About 160,000 went in the UK in 1983, short of the 350,000 the company had predicted, and about 50,000 in France, where it was the best-selling home computer that year and was voted ordinateur de l'année (computer of the year) for 1983. It launched there at 2,000 FF and later fell to 1,000 FF.

The weak points were the small rubbery keyboard, the tape loader and the first ROM. BASIC 1.0's tape verify routine was faulty, so programs saved by users could fail to load again, and several other bugs were left for the next ROM.

On 13 October 1983 a fire at the Kenure Plastics factory in Berkshire, where the machines were made, destroyed about 7,000 Orics. Production moved and restarted quickly; Personal Computer News reported it under the headline "Oric lit up".

Edenspring and the Atmos (1984) #

Late in 1983 Edenspring Investments bought the company and put £4m into it. The result was the Oric Atmos, launched in February 1984: the same board in a black and red case with a proper keyboard, and the BASIC 1.1 ROM, which fixed most of 1.0's bugs but not the tape verify. 1.1 also moved some ROM routines, so not every Oric-1 program runs on an Atmos, and many tapes carried a 1.0 version on one side and a 1.1 version on the other. Oric-1 owners could fit the new ROM in a spare socket with a switch between the two.

The Atmos was France's computer of the year for 1984, and fell there from 1,990 FF to 990 FF. The French article counts 27,000 Atmos sold between February and June 1984, and an installed base in France of about 120,000.

The peripherals promised since the Oric-1 arrived during 1984:

Peripheral What it was
Microdisc 3-inch floppy drive, summer 1984; about 3,600 FF in France
MCP-40 Four-colour pen plotter and printer
Modem Released alongside the drive and printer
Prestel adaptor The first Oric videotext adaptor, with little software

The Microdisc had been announced for the autumn of 1983 and arrived nearly a year late, at more than three times the price of the computer. Its ROM can be switched out, which makes the 16K of RAM under the BASIC ROM usable by the disk operating system. The MCP-40's mechanism was made by Alps and shared with the Atari 1020, the Commodore 1520 and others.

The Stratos and the Receivers (1985) #

Early in 1985 Oric announced several new models, among them IBM-compatible and MSX-compatible machines. On 1 February it showed the Oric Stratos (also called the IQ164) at the Frankfurt computer show. The next day, 2 February, Edenspring put Oric International into receivership.

The French company Eureka Informatique took over the French business on 1 June 1985 and carried on with the Stratos design. In November 1985 Eureka released SEDORIC, a disk operating system by Fabrice Broche and Denis Sebbag, which became the standard DOS for Oric disk users.

Eureka and the Telestrat (1986–1987) #

Eureka's Stratos became the Oric Telestrat, launched in France in April 1986 at 3,990 FF. It kept the Atmos's CPU, graphics and sound, had 64K of RAM, a disk drive as standard and more ports, and was aimed at Minitel, the French videotext network, with a Minitel port and telematic software built in. Atmos software ran through a cartridge, and a compiled BASIC, Hyper-BASIC, came on another. About 6,000 were sold, all in France.

Eureka announced a Telestrat 2 in September 1987, then went into receivership in December 1987, the second and final end of Oric. The French article says remaining Telestrats were sold until December 1988.

Clones #

The Atmos design outlived the company in Eastern Europe:

Clone Country Differences
Pravetz 8D Bulgaria 1985–1991; white case, mechanical keys, internal supply
Nova 64 Yugoslavia Licensed Atmos; only the logo changed

The Pravetz 8D's patched ROM gives Latin letters in upper case and Cyrillic in lower case, with a Caps Lock key to switch. In 1987–88 Borislav Zahariev added an Apple Disk II compatible interface and a DOS, DOS-8D.

Software, Magazines and Sales #

The Oric.org archive counts 589 commercially released games from 1983 to 1987. The early titles were mostly British: Tansoft, IJK, PSS, Level 9, Microdeal, Artic and others. From 1984 the market and the software became French: Loriciels, ERE Informatique, Cobra Soft, Infogrames, Micropuce, Norsoft and many smaller houses wrote for the Oric long after British publishers had moved on.

The magazines followed the same path, from Britain's Oric User Monthly to France's Théoric and Micro'Oric, and later CEO-Mag, the Club Europe Oric's magazine, which is still published.

Totals are uncertain. The English article gives 210,000 Oric-1s, most of them in 1983; the French article gives a little under 400,000 Orics of all models across Europe.

Timeline #

Year Event
1979 Tangerine Computer Systems founded in St Ives
1982 Oric Products International set up (April)
1982 Oric-1 launched in the UK: £129 (16K), £169 (48K)
1983 ~160,000 sold in the UK and ~50,000 in France
1983 Oric-1 is France's computer of the year
1983 Factory fire destroys about 7,000 machines (13 October)
1983 Edenspring Investments buys the company, invests £4m
1984 Oric Atmos (February): real keyboard, ROM V1.1
1984 Atmos is France's computer of the year
1984 Microdisc drive, MCP-40 plotter, modem released
1985 Stratos shown at Frankfurt (1 Feb); receivership (2 Feb)
1985 Eureka takes over in France (June); SEDORIC (November)
1985 Pravetz 8D clone in production in Bulgaria
1986 Telestrat (April): 64K, disk drive, Minitel
1987 Telestrat 2 announced; final receivership (December)

The Oric Today #

The Oric has one of the most active communities of any 8-bit machine, centred in France and Britain. The Club Europe Oric (CEO) publishes CEO-Mag and runs oric.org, the software archive, with its forum at forums.oric.org. Defence Force holds manuals, hardware notes and new software.

Emulation began with Fabrice Francès's Euphoric for MS-DOS. Today Oricutron (Peter Gordon), Clock Signal (Tom Harte) and Auric (Anders Piniesjö) run the original tapes and disks; the tech specs appendix has notes on running Auric.

New hardware keeps real machines in use: Erebus replaces the tape deck with an SD card of .tap files, Cumulus replaces the Microdisc with SD card disk images, and the Twilighte board adds 512K of RAM, an EEPROM, USB and SD card loading and joystick ports. LOCI, a newer add-on, has its own file manager and software on oric.org.

Markdown source: docs/oric_specs.md

Oric Tech Specs #

The hardware of the Oric-1 and Atmos for readers who know the C64: the parts, the memory map, how the screen and the sound chip work, and how to run Oric software today. The story of the machines is in the previous appendix, History of Oric. The figures are drawn by docs/tools/render_oric.py, and the BASIC examples were run on the Atmos ROM (BASIC 1.1) in the Auric emulator: all ran without errors, and the drawings and the POKE came out as described.

Specifications #

Part Oric-1 and Atmos
CPU 6502A at 1 MHz
RAM 16K or 48K (64K fitted; 16K hides under the ROM)
ROM 16K: Oric Extended BASIC 1.0 (Atmos 1.1)
Video ULA (HCS 10017): TEXT, LORES, HIRES modes
Colours 8, set by serial attributes
Sound General Instrument AY-3-8912, 3 tone + noise
I/O 6522 VIA: keyboard, tape, printer, AY bus
Keyboard 57 keys; rubber on the Oric-1, moving on the Atmos
Storage Cassette at 300 or 2400 baud
Video out RGB (5-pin DIN) and UHF RF
Other ports Centronics printer, expansion edge connector
Power External 9 V supply

The Models #

Every Oric shares the same core: a 6502A, the ULA's video and the AY sound chip. The models differ in RAM, ROM and keyboard:

Model Year RAM ROM and keyboard
Oric-1 1982 16K, 48K BASIC 1.0; small hard-key keyboard
Atmos 1984 48K BASIC 1.1; full-travel keyboard
Stratos 1985 64K Shown at Frankfurt; became the Telestrat
Telestrat 1986 64K Disk drive, Minitel port, cartridges
Pravetz 8D 1985 48K Atmos clone; Latin and Cyrillic ROM

Storage #

Device Medium Notes
Cassette Audio tape, .tap file 2400 baud by default; 300 baud with ,S (slow)
Microdisc 3-inch floppy Oric's drive, 1984; Oric DOS, later SEDORIC
Jasmin Floppy French third-party drive with its own DOS (TDOS)

Disk systems page the BASIC ROM out to use the 16K of RAM under it, which is why only 48K of the 64K fitted is free from BASIC. The Telestrat came with a drive as standard.

Memory Map #

The map of a 48K machine, as the ROM uses it:

Range Holds
$0000–$00FF Zero page (ROM workspace and program variables)
$0100–$01FF 6502 stack
$0200–$02FF ROM workspace (key buffer, vectors)
$0300–$03FF I/O: the 6522 VIA at $0300–$030F
$0400–$97FF Free RAM (BASIC programs start at $0501)
$9800–$9FFF Character sets while in HIRES
$A000–$BF3F HIRES screen: 200 lines of 40 bytes
$B400–$B7FF Standard character set (TEXT mode)
$B800–$BB7F Alternate character set (TEXT mode)
$BB80–$BFDF TEXT screen: 28 rows of 40 bytes
$C000–$FFFF ROM

The TEXT screen and its character sets sit inside the HIRES area: switching to HIRES moves the character sets down to $9800 and overwrites them, and only the bottom three text rows stay on screen.

Graphics #

The ULA reads one byte per 6-pixel cell, 40 cells to a line, and has no colour memory of its own. Colour is set by serial attributes: control bytes placed in the screen itself. An attribute takes up a cell, shows as a blank cell in the current paper colour, and changes the ink, paper or text style from that cell to the end of the line. Every line starts again as white ink on black paper.

0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
Black Red Green Yellow Blue Magenta Cyan White

A colour's number is its RGB bits: bit 0 red, bit 1 green, bit 2 blue.

Serial Attributes #

A screen byte whose bits 6 and 5 are both clear is an attribute; its low five bits say which:

Value Sets
0–7 Ink colour
8–15 Text style: bit 0 alternate set, bit 1 double, bit 2 blink
16–23 Paper colour (value − 16)
24–31 Video mode: bit 2 HIRES, bit 1 50 Hz

Bit 7 of any screen byte inverts its cell: ink and paper are each replaced by 7 minus their value. That is the only way to get a third colour into a cell without spending a cell on an attribute.

The strip below is one HIRES line of twelve cells, decoded as the ULA does (the grey ruler marks the cells):

Cell Byte Effect
1 $14 Paper blue (20); the cell itself shows blue
2 $03 Ink yellow; shows blue
3 $7F Six pixels on: solid yellow
4 $55 Pixels 010101: yellow on blue
5 $01 Ink red; a blue gap
6–7 $7F $6A Solid red, then 101010
8 $10 Paper black
9 $06 Ink cyan; shows black
10 $7F Solid cyan
11 $FF Solid, inverted: 7 − cyan (6) = red
12 $40 No pixels: black paper

This is the Oric's version of attribute clash: a 6-pixel cell can hold only two colours, and changing either costs a blank cell. Games work round it by changing colour where the picture is blank anyway, by keeping each line to one or two colours, and by using the inverse bit.

The Three Modes #

Mode Resolution Cell
TEXT 40 × 28 characters Character code, 6 × 8 from a character set
LORES 40 × 28 blocks Block graphics, 2 × 3 per cell
HIRES 240 × 200, plus 3 text rows Bit 6 set: six pixels, bit 5 leftmost

Both character sets are in RAM, so every character can be redefined: a game can turn the alternate set into its own graphics and still have letters in the standard set. Double height prints the top half of each character on even rows and the bottom half on odd rows, so a double-height line is the same text written on two rows.

From BASIC #

Oric BASIC has commands for each mode. HIRES draws with a graphics cursor; the last parameter is the foreground mode (0 paper, 1 ink, 2 invert, 3 move only):

10 HIRES
20 INK 6:PAPER 0
30 CURSET 120,100,1:CIRCLE 60,1
40 CURSET 20,20,1:DRAW 200,0,1:DRAW 0,160,1
50 FOR X=0 TO 239 STEP 4:CURSET X,199,1:DRAW 0,-20,2:NEXT
60 PRINT "HELLO FROM THE TEXT ROWS"

TEXT returns to text mode and LORES 0 or LORES 1 selects block graphics with the standard or alternate set. Attributes can be poked straight into the screen: POKE #BB80+40*5,17 makes row 5 red paper from its first cell.

The program above as Auric draws it. The three text rows keep their own paper and ink, set by BASIC, and the PRINT output has scrolled away, leaving Ready:

Sound #

The AY-3-8912 is General Instrument's AY-3-8910 (the MSX's sound chip) in a smaller package with one I/O port instead of two; the ZX Spectrum 128 and the Amstrad CPC use the same part. On the Oric it is clocked at 1 MHz.

Feature AY-3-8912 on the Oric
Tone Channels A, B, C: square waves, 12-bit period
Pitch 1 MHz ÷ (16 × period): ~15 Hz (period 4095) up to 62.5 kHz
Noise One generator, 5-bit period, mixable into any channel
Volume 0–15 per channel, or the envelope
Envelope One shared generator: 16-bit period, 16 shapes
I/O port Port A: drives the keyboard's column lines on the Oric

Registers #

Register Holds
R0–R1 Channel A tone period (fine, coarse 4 bits)
R2–R3 Channel B tone period
R4–R5 Channel C tone period
R6 Noise period, 0–31
R7 Mixer: tone off (bits 0–2), noise off (3–5), port A out (6)
R8–R10 Volume 0–15; bit 4 hands the channel to the envelope
R11–R12 Envelope period (fine, coarse)
R13 Envelope shape
R14 I/O port A

One envelope cycle lasts 256 × period µs at 1 MHz: from 0.26 ms to about 16.8 s. A period of $1904 (6404), for example, gives a single fall of about 1.6 s, long enough for an explosion.

Shapes 0–3 and 4–7 are one fall or one rise and then silence; 8–15 repeat or hold, set by R13's bits: continue (3), attack (2), alternate (1) and hold (0).

How the Oric Reaches the Chip #

The AY is not memory-mapped. Its data bus hangs off the VIA's port A and its two bus-control lines off the VIA's CA2 and CB2 outputs (set through the PCR at $030C), so every register write is two VIA operations: select the register, then write the value. Because the keyboard's column lines come from the AY's own I/O port, reading the keyboard also goes through the AY, which is why R7 bit 6 must stay set.

From BASIC #

10 PING:WAIT 50:SHOOT:WAIT 50:EXPLODE:WAIT 50:ZAP
20 SOUND 1,500,10
30 MUSIC 2,3,5,10
40 PLAY 3,0,1,2000

PING, SHOOT, EXPLODE and ZAP are ready-made effects. SOUND channel,period,volume plays a tone (channels 1–3) or noise (4–6); MUSIC channel,octave,note,volume plays a note (octave 0–6, note 1–12 from C); PLAY tone,noise, mode,period switches channels on (bit masks) and starts the envelope. A volume of 0 hands the channel to the envelope.

Running Oric Software in an Emulator #

Oric tapes, saved as .tap files, run in any Oric emulator that reads them. Two good choices are Auric, used to check the BASIC examples above, and Oricutron, the long-standing multi-platform emulator.

The ROMs #

No emulator ships the Oric ROMs. They are archived at oric.free.fr/ROMS, one zip per ROM. Auric looks for three files in its ROMS/ folder, under these names; the SHA1 sums are the ones its ROMS/README_ROMS.md lists as tested:

Auric file From the archive Machine SHA1
basic10.rom Basic1.0.zip Oric-1, BASIC 1.0 333116e6884d85aaa4dfc7578a91cceeea66d016
basic11b.rom Basic1.1.zip Atmos, BASIC 1.1 9451a1a09d8f75944dbd6f91193fc360f1de80ac
microdis.rom Oricdisc.zip Microdisc drive 0d2ef6e67322f48f4b7e08d8bbe68827e2074561

Each archive unzips to one ROM, which is renamed to the name in the first column and can be checked with shasum. Auric refuses to start unless all three are present, even with no disk in use: the Microdisc ROM is only switched in when a disk image is given, but the file is loaded at start-up.

Building and Running Auric #

Auric builds with CMake against four libraries, which Homebrew provides on macOS (argparse, spdlog, sdl3, yaml-cpp; the repository's doc/BUILD_HOST.md has the details and a vcpkg alternative):

git clone https://github.com/pugo/Auric.git
cd Auric && mkdir build && cd build && cmake .. && make -j10

Auric runs from the Auric folder, since it reads auric.yaml and ROMS/ from the current directory. The binary may be build/auric or build/src/auric, depending on the build. --oric1 selects the Oric-1 ROM (the default is the Atmos), which early tapes written for the Oric-1 may need, and --tape loads and starts a tape:

cd Auric && ./build/src/auric --oric1 --tape /path/to/game.tap

F1 opens Auric's menu (settings, tape and disk images, rewind), Shift-Ctrl-W toggles warp speed and Shift-Ctrl-R resets. On a real Oric, or with autostart turned off, CLOAD"" and Return load the tape.
